problems.one_liner: A size-k min-heap, or quickselect, both avoid a full sort.
problems.core_objective: Return the k-th largest element of an array, counting the largest as first.
problems.bounds: 1 <= k <= nums.length <= 2e4, so k is always valid. Values are ints, so `heapq.nlargest` and `sorted` both work, but the O(n log n) sort is avoidable.

approaches.name: · Min-heap of size k (best)
approaches.aha: 1. Push each value; if len(heap) > k, heappop (removes the smallest — the value that just fell out of the top-k). 2. After the sweep, heap[0] is the k-th largest.
approaches.why: one push (and at most one pop) per element; hence the stated bounds.

approaches.name: · Quickselect (Hoare's partition)
approaches.aha: Partition around a pivot; if the pivot lands at index len-k it IS the answer; otherwise recurse into the correct half. O(n) average. --------------------------------------------------------------------- DEEP DIVE · Why a MIN-heap, not a max-heap A max-heap lets you pop the largest repeatedly, but the heap "loses" the k-th largest once you pop it. The min-heap of size k tracks the boundary of the top-k: new elements smaller than the root are ignored implicitly by the pop. Python's heapq is a min-heap natively — zero configuration. --------------------------------------------------------------------- TIME COMPLEXITY : O(n log k) — n pushes, each O(log k). MEMORY COMPLEXITY: O(k) — the heap holds at most k values. =====================================================================
approaches.py:
pivot = nums[random.randint(lo, hi)]
left, mid, right = lo, lo, hi
while mid <= right:              # 3-way partition
    if nums[mid] < pivot:
        nums[left], nums[mid] = nums[mid], nums[left]
        left += 1; mid += 1
    elif nums[mid] > pivot:
        nums[mid], nums[right] = nums[right], nums[mid]
approaches.time: O(n log k)   — n pushes, each O(log k).
approaches.space: O(k)          — the heap holds at most k values.
approaches.why: Follows directly from the traversal count: O(n log k)   — n pushes, each O(log k). time, O(k)          — the heap holds at most k values. space.

problems.diagram:
nums = [3,2,1,5,6,4], k = 2 -> 5

 heap of size k (a MIN-heap keeps the k LARGEST):
   push 3 -> [3]
   push 2 -> [2,3]
   push 1 -> [1,3,2]
   push 5 -> [1,5,2,3]  size 4 > k, pop MIN 1 -> [2,5,3]
   push 6 -> [2,5,3,6]  size 4 > k, pop MIN 2 -> [3,5,6]
   push 4 -> [3,4,6,5]  size 4 > k, pop MIN 3 -> [4,5,6]
   heap top = 4 = SMALLEST of the 4 largest {4,5,6}? there
   are only 4 kept -> top 4, we want 2nd largest of 6
   numbers: largest=6, 2nd=5.
   -> heapify(heap); return heap[0]  -> need the MIN of the
      k largest, i.e. pop the min once then the top is the 2nd.
   Correct form: heapq.nlargest(k, nums)[-1]

  quickselect: partition around a pivot, recurse into the
  side that contains index len-k, average O(n).
problems.cpp_vs_py:
A max-heap lets you pop the largest repeatedly, but the heap "loses" the k-th largest once you pop it. The min-heap of size k tracks the boundary of the top-k: new elements smaller than the root are ignored implicitly by the pop. Python's heapq is a min-heap natively — zero configuration. --------------------------------------------------------------------- TIME COMPLEXITY : O(n log k) — n pushes, each O(log k).

=====================================================================
cpp_alts: `std::nth_element(nums.begin(), nums.begin() + k - 1, nums.end(), greater<int>())` then `nums[k-1]` is the answer: $O(n)$ average, no extra memory.
`std::partial_sort` is the deterministic cousin of nth_element: $O(n \log k)$, and a better worst case.
A heap of size k is $O(n \log k)$ and $O(k)$ space -- the right answer when memory is constrained.
py_alts: `heapq.nlargest(k, nums)[-1]` is the idiomatic one-liner and is C-implemented.
`sorted(nums, reverse=True)[k-1]` is $O(n \log n)$ -- correct, and worth naming as the baseline.
For small k and small n, `max` in a loop is actually competitive because the interpreter overhead is amortised over few calls.
problems.trap: Off-by-one on the index: the k-th largest is at sorted index k-1, not k. Also, using a max-heap of size k and returning its top gives the k-th SMALLEST, not largest -- the heap must be a MIN-heap of the k largest.
problems.invariant: After processing any prefix of the array, the heap contains the k largest elements of that prefix (or all of them if the prefix is shorter than k). Each push-then-pop-min preserves this, so at the end the heap's minimum is the k-th largest of the whole array.

questions.q: Why a min-heap of size k rather than a max-heap?
questions.a: Because you want to keep the k largest, so you need to know which retained element is the weakest -- the minimum. A max-heap's top would be the largest retained, which tells you nothing about whether a new element belongs in the set.

That the first k positions hold the k largest elements as an unordered set, in linear average time. It does not sort them, which is exactly what this problem allows since the answer is a single value.

Heap: $O(n \log k)$ time, $O(k)$ space. nth_element: $O(n)$ average but $O(n^2)$ worst case on adversarial pivots, with $O(1)$ space. Sorting: $O(n \log n)$ time, and C++'s in-place sort is $O(\log n)$ stack.

problems.one_liner: Two heaps with a size invariant; the answer is the max-heap top.
problems.core_objective: Support adding an integer and retrieving the median of all values added so far in amortized O(1) each.
problems.bounds: Up to 1e5 operations and values up to 1e5, so the median is an integer and needs no rounding. Odd and even counts alternate, so the balancing logic must handle both.

approaches.name: · Two heaps (best)
approaches.aha: 1. addNum: push to the lower max-heap; rebalance by moving the boundary element if lower's top exceeds upper's top. 2. findMedian: equal sizes -> mean of both tops; else top of the taller heap.
approaches.why: one push (and at most one pop) per element; hence the stated bounds.

approaches.name: · Bisect-insert into a sorted list (baseline)
approaches.aha: data.insert(bisect_left(data, v), v) is O(n) per add due to the memmove — fine for small n, hopeless at scale. --------------------------------------------------------------------- DEEP DIVE · The balance invariant Invariants after every add: (a) len(lower) == len(upper) or len(lower) == len(upper) + 1; (b) max(lower) <= min(upper). Fixing (b): when lower[-1] (its max, via -lower[0]) > upper[0], swap the two tops. Fixing (a): if upper ever gets taller, migrate its minimum to the lower heap. Median always reads off the seam. --------------------------------------------------------------------- TIME COMPLEXITY : O(log n) per addNum ; O(1) findMedian. MEMORY COMPLEXITY: O(n). =====================================================================
approaches.py:
self.data = []
self.data.insert(bisect.bisect_left(self.data, num), num)
n = len(self.data)
if n % 2:
    return self.data[n // 2]
return (self.data[n // 2 - 1] + self.data[n // 2]) / 2.0
approaches.time: O(log n) per addNum ; O(1) findMedian.
approaches.why: the sort dominates; the post-sort scan is linear; hence the stated bounds.

problems.diagram:
add 1, 2, 3, 4, 5

   lower (MAX-heap)   upper (MIN-heap)   median
   ---- ------------  ----------------  -------
   1    [1]          []                1   (1 = 1)
   2    [1]          [2]               1   (even -> low)
   3    [2,1]        [3]               2   (3 = 2)
   4    [2,1]        [3,4]             2   (even -> low)
   5    [3,1,2]      [4,5]             3   (5 = 3)

   INVARIANT: len(lower) == len(upper)          or
              len(lower) == len(upper) + 1
   EVERY element of lower <= EVERY element of upper

   median:
     odd  count -> lower[0]      (the max-heap top)
     even count -> (-lower[0] + upper[0]) / 2

   python's heapq is MIN-only, so lower stores NEGATED
   values and lower[0] is the true maximum.
problems.cpp_vs_py:
Invariants after every add: (a) len(lower) == len(upper) or len(lower) == len(upper) + 1; (b) max(lower) <= min(upper). Fixing (b): when lower[-1] (its max, via -lower[0]) > upper[0], swap the two tops. Fixing (a): if upper ever gets taller, migrate its minimum to the lower heap. Median always reads off the seam. --------------------------------------------------------------------- TIME COMPLEXITY : O(log n) per addNum ; O(1) findMedian.

=====================================================================
cpp_alts: `std::priority_queue<int>` (max) and `std::priority_queue<int, vector<int>, greater<int>>` (min) are the natural pair -- no negation needed.
`__gnu_pbds::rb_tree` with two order-statistics iterators would also work but is heavier than heaps.
py_alts: heapq is min-only: push negated values into `lower` and read `-lower[0]` as the maximum.
`heapq.heappush` / `heappushpop` are C-level; keeping the balance check outside the heap calls matters more than the choice of push variant.
problems.trap: Getting the parity convention backwards -- returning `upper[0]` for an odd count. The whole design hinges on `lower` always holding the extra element when the count is odd, so that the median is always accessible at `lower[0]`.
problems.invariant: `len(lower) == len(upper)` or `len(lower) == len(upper) + 1`, and `max(lower) <= min(upper)`. Together these make the median a read of one or two heap tops, and they are preserved by inserting into `lower` then moving its top to `upper` when `lower` grows too large.

questions.q: Why does `lower` hold the extra element when the count is odd?
questions.a: So the median is always `lower`'s maximum. If the smaller half holds one more element, its top is exactly the middle value of the sorted sequence -- for both parities, with a two-term average only when even.

questions.q: Why is inserting into `lower` then rebalancing correct?
questions.a: Adding to `lower` can only violate the ordering invariant if `lower` was empty or `upper` was non-empty and the new value exceeds `upper`'s minimum. In both cases moving `lower`'s maximum to `upper` restores the ordering, and fixing the sizes then restores the count invariant.
$O(n)$ -- every value ever added is retained, split across the two heaps. That is unavoidable: the median depends on the whole multiset, so nothing can be discarded.

problems.one_liner: Follow graph plus a timestamp-ordered feed per user.
problems.core_objective: Design a Twitter-like API supporting follow, unfollow, post, and a user's recent posts including those of followed users.
problems.bounds: At most 1e5 operations and 5e9 user IDs, so IDs must be long and follow sets must be hash-based. The feed is capped at 10 tweets, which is the key constraint that shapes the data structures.

approaches.name: · Merge-k with a max-heap (best)
approaches.aha: Push the newest tweet of every followed user; pop the max; then push that user's next-newest; stop at 10. Heap stays ≤ #follows.
approaches.py:
self.tweets = collections.defaultdict(list)   # user -> [(clock, id)]
self.follows = collections.defaultdict(set)
self.clock = 0
self.tweets[userId].append((self.clock, tweetId))
self.clock += 1
if followerId != followeeId:
    self.follows[followerId].add(followeeId)
self.follows[followerId].discard(followeeId)
approaches.why: one push (and at most one pop) per element; hence the stated bounds.

approaches.name: · Gather-all + sort (baseline)
approaches.aha: Collect every tweet of every followed user, sort by time desc. --------------------------------------------------------------------- DEEP DIVE · k-way merge vs flat sort Flat: O(F·K log(F·K)) with F follows and K tweets each. Merge-k: O(F log F) per popped tweet — the classic external-sort pattern. Ties: we never pop more than one tweet of a user before its successor enters the heap, so ordering stays strictly chronological. The clock counts up per post, so "most recent" == "largest clock". --------------------------------------------------------------------- TIME COMPLEXITY : getNewsFeed O(F log F); post/follow O(1). MEMORY COMPLEXITY: O(T) for T tweets + follow edges. =====================================================================
approaches.py:
self.all = collections.defaultdict(list)
self.follows = collections.defaultdict(set)
self.clock = 0
self.all[userId].append((self.clock, tweetId))
self.clock += 1
if followerId != followeeId:
    self.follows[followerId].add(followeeId)
self.follows[followerId].discard(followeeId)
approaches.time: getNewsFeed O(F log F); post/follow O(1).
approaches.space: O(T) for T tweets + follow edges.
approaches.why: the sort dominates; the post-sort scan is linear; hence the stated bounds.

problems.diagram:
post(1, [2,3])

   followers: { 1: {2,3} }
   tweets[tweetId] = { id:1, uid:1, ts:... }
   userTweets[1] = heap of tweet ids by ts

   getRecent(3):
     candidates = {2,3} U self(3)
     for each u in candidates:
        merge the top of userTweets[u] into the result heap
     pop the largest ts until 10 collected or all heaps empty

   k = 10 CAP: you never need the whole timeline, so
   per-user heaps are only drained lazily, at most 10 times.
   That is what makes O(k log k)-ish work per query instead of
   O(total tweets).

   follow(a,b):  followers[a].add(b)
   unfollow(a,b): followers[a].discard(b)   (a==b is a no-op)
   post: push to that user's heap, incrementing the global clock
problems.cpp_vs_py:
Flat: O(F·K log(F·K)) with F follows and K tweets each. Merge-k: O(F log F) per popped tweet — the classic external-sort pattern. Ties: we never pop more than one tweet of a user before its successor enters the heap, so ordering stays strictly chronological. The clock counts up per post, so "most recent" == "largest clock". --------------------------------------------------------------------- TIME COMPLEXITY : getNewsFeed O(F log F); post/follow O(1).

=====================================================================
cpp_alts: `unordered_map<int, unordered_set<int>>` for the follow graph; a set is required because unfollow must be $O(1)$ and duplicates must be idempotent.
`multiset<pair<ts, tweetId>>` per user gives ordered access with erase-by-key, which a heap cannot do.
`map<int, ...>` instead of unordered only if you need ordered user iteration, which the API does not require.
py_alts: `defaultdict(set)` for the follow graph; `set` gives O(1) follow/unfollow and automatic dedupe.
`OrderedDict` per user keyed by timestamp keeps insertion order without a heap, at O(1) `move_to_end` and popitem.
`heapq.merge(*[userTweets[u] for u in candidates])` is a lazy k-way merge -- the cleanest expression of the query.
problems.trap: Returning the 10 most recent tweets of ALL followed users rather than per-user merges, and ignoring the self-inclusion rule. A user always sees their own tweets, and duplicates must not appear if they follow someone who also follows them.
problems.invariant: Each user's tweet container is ordered newest-first, so the newest tweet overall among a candidate set is the maximum of the per-user heads. Merging those heads and popping 10 times therefore yields exactly the 10 newest, and the merge touches at most 10 nodes per container.

questions.q: Why does the k=10 cap make this tractable?
questions.a: Without it you would need to sort every tweet by every followed user -- potentially unbounded work. With the cap, a k-way merge over per-user sorted streams needs at most k pops, each $O(\log |F|)$ where F is the follow count. The cap is what turns an unbounded query into a bounded one.

questions.q: What structure per user, and why?
questions.a: A heap, multiset, or ordered dict keyed by timestamp, all of which support newest-first access in $O(1)$. A plain list would need insertion in the middle ($O(n)$) unless you keep it sorted, which is worse. The requirement is ordered access to the newest element, not arbitrary access.

questions.q: How do you make unfollow O(1)?
questions.a: Store each user's following set as a hash set, not a list. Deletion from a set is expected $O(1)$, and re-following is idempotent. A list would need a scan, which is why the set is load-bearing rather than incidental.

problems.core_objective: Return the minimum number of time units to run all tasks given a non-negative cooldown between identical tasks.
problems.bounds: 1 <= tasks.length <= 1e4 and 1 <= n <= tasks.length, so the answer fits comfortably in int. Cooldown n can exceed the alphabet size, in which case the answer is just the task count.

approaches.name: · Math formula (best)
approaches.aha: m = max frequency, c = count of tasks with frequency m. answer = max((m - 1) * (n + 1) + c, len(tasks)).
approaches.py:
cnt = collections.Counter(tasks)
m = max(cnt.values())
c = sum(1 for v in cnt.values() if v == m)
return max((m - 1) * (n + 1) + c, len(tasks))
approaches.why: constant time after one counting pass; hence the stated bounds.

approaches.name: · Heap simulation
approaches.aha: Max-heap of remaining counts + FIFO cooldown queue; every second run the most frequent available task, park it for n seconds. --------------------------------------------------------------------- DEEP DIVE · Why the formula is exact The busiest task T appears m times; between consecutive copies we need n other/ idle slots — that core costs (m-1)(n+1) units, and the LAST row fits all c tasks that tie with T. Filling the core gaps with the remaining tasks is always possible greedily, so the lower bound is tight. If tasks alone already fill every slot (len(tasks) larger), no idle is needed. O(1) beats O(26 log 26). --------------------------------------------------------------------- TIME COMPLEXITY : O(1) — one pass over 26 counters. MEMORY COMPLEXITY: O(1). =====================================================================
approaches.py:
cnt = collections.Counter(tasks)
heap = [-v for v in cnt.values()]
heapq.heapify(heap)
cooldown = collections.deque()     # (remaining, readyAt)
t = 0
while heap or cooldown:
    t += 1
    if heap:
approaches.why: one push (and at most one pop) per element; hence the stated bounds.

problems.diagram:
tasks = [A,A,A,B,B,C,C,C], n = 2  -> answer 7

  frequencies: A:3 B:2 C:3
  maxFreq = 3, maxFreqCount = 2 (A and C)
  formula = (3-1) * (7-2) + 3 = 10 + 3 = 13 ? NO
  correct: (maxFreq-1)*(n - maxFreqCount) + maxFreq
         = (3-1)*(7-2) + 3 = 13   ... but expected 7?

  Recompute: n = 2 cooldown.
   A . . A . . A      frames of length 3, 2 frames
   B . . B
   C . . C
   total = 2*3 + 1 = 7
  formula with maxFreq=3, maxFreqCount=2, len=7:
   (3-1)*(7-2) + 3 = 13  is wrong; the correct form is
   (maxFreq-1)*(n - maxFreqCount) + maxFreqCount
   (3-1)*(7-2) + 2 = 12  also wrong for this example because
   the OTHER tasks fill the gaps.

  The derivation:
   maxFreq-1 frames are needed, each frame has length n.
   The most frequent tasks occupy maxFreqCount slots per frame.
   Everything else (len - maxFreq*maxFreqCount tasks) fills the
   remaining slack. Result =
     max( len, (maxFreq-1)*n + maxFreqCount )
problems.cpp_vs_py:
The busiest task T appears m times; between consecutive copies we need n other/ idle slots — that core costs (m-1)(n+1) units, and the LAST row fits all c tasks that tie with T. Filling the core gaps with the remaining tasks is always possible greedily, so the lower bound is tight. If tasks alone already fill every slot (len(tasks) larger), no idle is needed. O(1) beats O(26 log 26). --------------------------------------------------------------------- TIME COMPLEXITY : O(1) — one pass over 26 counters.

=====================================================================
cpp_alts: A 26-element frequency array plus two running maxima is $O(T + 26)$ with no map.
The heap simulation is $O(T \log 26)$ and is more obviously correct, which is why it is the fallback.
py_alts: `Counter(tasks).values()` plus `max`/`count` gives the two quantities in one pass.
The heap simulation with `Counter` and `list.index` on a 26-slot cooldown array is readable and fast enough.
problems.trap: Using the widely-copied formula `(maxFreq-1)*(n-maxFreqCount) + maxFreq` without checking it against a worked example. It is not correct in general; the frame-based derivation gives `max(len, (maxFreq-1)*n + maxFreqCount)`.
problems.invariant: No schedule can be shorter than `len` tasks, and the cooldown forces at least `maxFreq - 1` separate frames of at least `n` units with `maxFreqCount` tasks pinned per frame. The answer is the max of those two lower bounds, and both are achievable.

questions.q: Why do the most frequent tasks define the frame count?
questions.a: A task occurring f times needs f-1 cooldowns between them, so it spans at least f slots. That forces at least maxFreq-1 frame boundaries, each of which must be at least n long or the cooldown would be violated.
When `(maxFreq-1)*n + maxFreqCount <= len`, i.e. the other tasks fill every frame completely. Then no idle slot is needed and the schedule runs back to back.

questions.q: Why is a heap simulation not necessary?
questions.a: Because the frame structure gives a closed-form lower bound that is achievable. The simulation is $O(T \log 26)$ and useful as a correctness check or when the cooldown structure is more complex, but it is strictly more work for no extra information.

problems.one_liner: Keep the top k in a min-heap; its root is the answer.
problems.core_objective: Return the k-th largest value seen so far in a stream, for every add.
problems.bounds: 1 <= k <= 500 <= n <= 1e4, so the heap never exceeds 500 and every operation is comfortably bounded. Values are non-negative ints.

approaches.name: · Min-heap of size k (best)
approaches.aha: Constructor: heapify nums, trim to size k by popping the root. add(v): heappush, pop if oversized, return heap[0].
approaches.py:
self.k = k
self.heap = nums[:]
heapq.heapify(self.heap)
while len(self.heap) > k:
    heapq.heappop(self.heap)
heapq.heappush(self.heap, val)
if len(self.heap) > self.k:
    heapq.heappop(self.heap)
approaches.why: one push (and at most one pop) per element; hence the stated bounds.

approaches.name: · Naive sorted list (baseline)
approaches.aha: Append and re-sort descending on every add; answer is index k-1. --------------------------------------------------------------------- DEEP DIVE · Why we can reject values forever Invariant: heap holds the k largest values of the stream. A new value ≤ heap[0] is ≤ every element in the top-k, so no matter how many future values arrive, this one can never rise into the top-k — discarding it loses nothing. Values > heap[0] replace the root (O(log k)) and keep the invariant. This "small values are dead on arrival" insight is the whole trick of streaming top-k. --------------------------------------------------------------------- TIME COMPLEXITY : O(log k) per add ; O(k) construction. MEMORY COMPLEXITY: O(k). =====================================================================
approaches.py:
self.k = k
self.data = sorted(nums, reverse=True)[:k]
self.data.append(val)
self.data.sort(reverse=True)
self.data = self.data[:self.k]
return self.data[self.k - 1]
approaches.time: O(log k) per add ; O(k) construction.
approaches.why: the sort dominates; the post-sort scan is linear; hence the stated bounds.

problems.diagram:
k = 3, adds: 4, 5, 8, 2, 3

  heap (size <= 3, MIN-heap of the k largest):
   add 4 -> {4}                 kth = 4
   add 5 -> {4,5}               kth = 4
   add 8 -> {4,5,8}             kth = 4
   add 2 -> {2,4,5,8} pop 2     -> {4,5,8}  kth = 4
   add 3 -> {3,4,5,8} pop 3     -> {4,5,8}  kth = 4

  heap root = MIN of the retained k = the k-th largest overall.

  invariant: |heap| == min(k, n) and heap contains the k largest
  values seen so far. Each add is one push plus at most one pop,
  so amortized O(log k).

  contrast with 215 (static array): there you may sort or
  quickselect; here the input is a stream, so nothing but the
  retained top k may be stored.
problems.cpp_vs_py:
Invariant: heap holds the k largest values of the stream. A new value ≤ heap[0] is ≤ every element in the top-k, so no matter how many future values arrive, this one can never rise into the top-k — discarding it loses nothing. Values > heap[0] replace the root (O(log k)) and keep the invariant. This "small values are dead on arrival" insight is the whole trick of streaming top-k. --------------------------------------------------------------------- TIME COMPLEXITY : O(log k) per add ; O(k) construction.

=====================================================================
cpp_alts: `priority_queue<int, vector<int>, greater<int>>` is a min-heap by default with the comparator -- exactly the structure needed.
A fixed `vector` of size k with manual sift is faster but far more code.
py_alts: `heapq.heappushpop(heap, x)` fuses push-and-pop into one C call and is faster than a separate push then conditional pop.
When the heap is already full, `heappushpop` returns the smallest; if x is larger than the root it is inserted and the old minimum is discarded in a single operation.
problems.trap: Using a MAX-heap of size k, whose top is the largest of the retained set -- that gives you the largest, not the k-th largest. Or returning `heap[0]` before the heap has reached size k.
problems.invariant: After each add, the heap holds exactly the k largest values seen so far (or all values if fewer than k have arrived), so its minimum is the k-th largest. `heappushpop` maintains this in one call because it only evicts when the new value exceeds the current minimum.

questions.q: Why can you discard the smaller elements permanently?
questions.a: Because at most k values ever matter for the answer, and only ever more values arrive. Once a value is not among the k largest, no future addition can promote it -- adding new elements only pushes the k-th largest upward. So discarded values are provably irrelevant.

questions.q: What if the heap is not yet full?
questions.a: Then every value so far is a candidate, and the answer is simply the heap's minimum. `heappushpop` handles this automatically: while `len(heap) < k` it behaves as a plain push.

questions.q: How does this differ from problem 215?
questions.a: 215 has the whole array available, so sorting ($O(n \log n)$) or `nth_element`/quickselect ($O(n)$) is possible. Here the input is a stream, so only the retained top k may be stored, which forces the $O(n \log k)$ heap.

problems.one_liner: Pop the two heaviest stones; a tie annihilates both.
problems.core_objective: Return the smallest possible weight of the remaining stone, or 0 if none remain.
problems.bounds: 1 <= stones.length <= 30 with weights 1..100, so at most 30 pops of a pair and an answer of at most 100. Weights are small enough that a counting bucket works too.

approaches.name: · Max-heap simulation (best)
approaches.aha: Negate every weight (heapq = min-heap). While ≥ 2 stones: pop two, smash, push back the difference as a negative if non-zero.
approaches.py:
heap = [-w for w in stones]
heapq.heapify(heap)
while len(heap) > 1:
    a = -heapq.heappop(heap)         # heaviest
    b = -heapq.heappop(heap)         # second heaviest
    if a != b:
        heapq.heappush(heap, -(a - b))
return -heap[0] if heap else 0
approaches.cpp:

cpp_alts: `priority_queue<int>` is a max-heap with no negation needed.
With weights <= 100 a `vector<int> count(101)` descending sweep gives $O(W + n)$ with no heap at all.
py_alts: heapq is min-only: store negated weights and read `-heapq.heappop(h)`.
The counting approach is elegant here: `for w in range(100, 0, -1)` and consume the count in pairs.
problems.trap: Continuing to pop twice when only one stone remains. The `while len(h) > 1` guard handles this; the bug is a `while h:` loop that pops twice unconditionally.
problems.invariant: The heap holds exactly the weights of the stones not yet smashed. Each iteration removes the two heaviest and inserts their difference, which is precisely the problem's operation, so the invariant is preserved and the final top is the minimum surviving weight.

questions.q: Why is the answer the heap's top rather than the sum?
questions.a: Because smashing two stones a >= b replaces them with a - b, and the total weight decreases by exactly 2b. Greedily smashing the two heaviest is optimal, and when the heap empties the answer is 0; when one stone remains its weight is the answer, not a sum.

The counting bucket becomes infeasible (the array would be too large) and you must fall back on the heap, which is $O(n \log n)$ and works for any magnitude. The bucket is purely an optimisation enabled by the weight bound.

Yes, and the exchange argument is short: if an optimal schedule does not smash the two heaviest together first, you can swap that pairing in without increasing the final weight, since the heavier stone can only ever reduce itself by pairing with something no heavier.
